newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai PM vows to revive economy, clean up politics.
newsitem.headline: Thai PM vows to revive economy, clean up politics.

text.p: Thailand's new government on Wednesday targeted resuscitation of the ailing economy and political reform as its key objectives but critics said the policy declaration lacked detail and a time frame for results.

In a 45-minute speech in parliament, Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh said a major priority of his week-old government would be to restore confidence in Thailand among local and foreign investors spooked by economic and political difficulties.
"The government plans to stabilise the economy, reduce the gap between rich and poor and create confidence among Thai and foreign investors," he said.

"It is going to reduce the problem of the trade deficit and the current account deficit by increasing revenue and foreign exchange and also reduce the state's unnecessary expenses and incompetent investments," he added.
Chavalit's administration was elected after polls last month.
Chavalit also pledged to speed up political reform, including a revision of the nation's constitution and a tightening of election rules to curb rampant vote-buying.
The premier had vowed during the election campaign to disband his government once a new constitution was ready.

Nearly 3,000 candidates nationwide are running in next week's election to fill the 76-member assembly that will draft the new constitution. Once the assembly starts work, it must complete the new charter and related laws within 18 months.
But the opposition Democratic Party's leader, Chuan Leekpai, told parliament the government's statement lacked specifics and failed to set measurable targets.
"If you really want to implement the policy just declared, one has to set specific measures and action plans on how to salvage the plunging economy," he said.
"Then the opposition and the people can follow the government's performance and assess after one year how much you have done of what you said," Chuan added.
Critics also said Chavalit's government failed to mention how it planned to stamp out rampant local corruption, illegal businesses, organised crime and prostitution.

"The government should have made clear its measures to crack down on corruption and organised crime such as prostitution rackets and drug trafficking," said Krikiat Pipataseritham of the Thai Chamber of Commerce University.
Corruption and organised crime are major national problems, according to a Chulalongkorn University study, and have been blamed for discouraging foreigners and locals from investing more in Thailand.

"Eight-five percent of the new government's policies were copied from the previous government and unfortunately this government has neither set a time frame for its action plan nor said what to do about corruption," said former premier Banharn Silpa-archa, whose unpopular government was forced out of office before the election.
